---
title: Multiple runs
jupyter: python3
---


Let's be honest, there isn't much you can do with a single sim run. So 99.9% of the time, you'll be wanting to run multiple simulations and compare them.

The easiest way to do this is with `ss.parallel()`, which, as the name suggests, runs the sims in parallel on your computer using all available cores. Sims passed as keywords are labeled with the keyword, which is the name of their scenario. Let's say we want to see what difference swapping the network makes:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
ss.options(jupyter=True) # Improve plot resolution

sim1 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks='random')
sim2 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks=ssl.RandomSafeNet())
msim = ss.parallel(random=sim1, randomsafe=sim2)
msim.plot()
```

`ss.parallel()` is just a wrapper for `ss.MultiSim().run()` (and note how we can pass arguments to all of the sims, e.g. `verbose=0` here). Sims given in a list are labeled by their own `label`:

```{python}
sim1 = ss.Sim(label='random', n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks='random')
sim2 = ss.Sim(label='randomsafe', n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks=ssl.RandomSafeNet())
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims=[sim1, sim2]).run(verbose=0)
msim.plot()
```

In most cases, this is the most efficient workflow: make some sims (potentially via a loop), and then run them. But there are some other common workflows as well.

## Many runs of one sim

A stochastic sim (one that runs as agents, or with the `'binomial'` or `'gillespie'` solver) gives a different answer each time it is run with a different random seed. `sim.run(n_runs=10)` runs it that many times, each with its own seed, and returns a MultiSim; it is a shortcut for `ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=10)`:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sir', networks='random', verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=10)
msim.plot()
```

`msim.plot()` shows the median of the runs and a 95% interval; `msim.plot(lines=True)` shows every run, which is how to see extinction or bimodality that a median hides:

```{python}
msim.plot(lines=True)
```

Every result of the runs is in `msim.results`, as the same result as for one sim, with a run axis first, so it can be summarized over the runs directly:

```{python}
res = msim.results.sir.n_I # One row per run
low, mid, high = res.quantiles([0.1, 0.5, 0.9]) # Quantiles over the runs
res.median().plot() # The median, as a result of one run
print(len(msim), res.shape)
```

`res.select(run=3)` is the result of one run, and `msim.sims` still holds the sims that were run.

## Scenarios

A scenario is a sim: it contains exactly the interventions passed to it. `sim.new()` makes a copy of a sim with something changed, which is the easiest way to make a scenario from a baseline. With `n_runs=`, each scenario is run that many times, and the runs of each scenario share their random numbers, so the difference between them is the effect of the intervention rather than noise. `msim.diff()` gives the difference of each scenario from the baseline, run by run:

```{python}
base = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2030', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.1), networks='random', verbose=0)
vaccine = ss.vaccinate(ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8), coverage=0.3, at=['2010'])
msim = ss.parallel(baseline=base, vaccine=base.new(interventions=vaccine), n_runs=5)
msim.plot()

averted = -msim.diff('baseline').vaccine.sis.infection.cum # Infections averted, one row per run
print(f'Infections averted by 2030: {averted.median()[-1]:,.0f}')
```

A result across scenarios can be selected by scenario, e.g. `msim.results.sis.prevalence.select(scenario='vaccine')`.

## Parameter sweeps

`ss.parallel()` also takes sets of parameter values to run a sim with: a dict with a list of values for each parameter. Each value is run `n_runs` times, and the values become coordinates of the runs, so they can be selected:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases=ss.SIR(beta=0.05), networks='random', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=[0.03, 0.05, 0.08]), n_runs=3)
print(msim.results.sir.n_I.runs) # The scenario and parameter values of each run
msim.results.sir.n_I.select(beta=0.08).quantiles().plot()
```

When there is more than one module, give the parameter with the module's name, e.g. `pars={'sir.beta': [0.03, 0.05]}`.

## Comparing sims

To compare sims side by side, use `msim.compare()`. By default this shows the summary of each sim (see `sim.summarize()`), with one column per sim; pass `t` to compare the results at a particular timestep index or date instead (dates are matched against each result's own timeline, so this works even if modules have different timesteps):

```{python}
s1 = ss.Sim(label='Low beta', n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2050', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), networks='random')
s2 = ss.Sim(label='High beta', n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2050', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.10), networks='random')
msim = ss.parallel(s1, s2, verbose=0)
msim.compare() # Compare the summaries
msim.compare(t='2030-01-01') # Compare the results on a particular date
```

Use `output=True` to get the comparison as a dataframe, or `msim.plot_compare()` to plot it as a bar chart, with one panel per result:

```{python}
msim.plot_compare()
```

## Combining, merging, and splitting

Several smaller sims can be treated as one larger population with `msim.combine()`, which returns a single sim. Results that scale with population size (e.g. counts) are summed, and other results (e.g. prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim's `total_pop`:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, diseases='sis', networks='random', verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=4)
combined = msim.combine() # Equivalent to a single sim with 4,000 agents
combined.plot()
```

You can also merge several MultiSims into one with `ss.MultiSim.merge()`, and split one into several with `msim.split()`. Each sim's label is the scenario of its runs, so a merged MultiSim plots each scenario with its uncertainty:

```{python}
m1 = ss.MultiSim(ss.Sim(label='Low beta', n_agents=2000, diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), networks='random'), n_runs=3)
m2 = ss.MultiSim(ss.Sim(label='High beta', n_agents=2000, diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.10), networks='random'), n_runs=3)
m1.run(verbose=0)
m2.run(verbose=0)

merged = ss.MultiSim.merge(m1, m2) # A MultiSim with 6 runs
merged.plot() # The median and interval of each scenario
m1, m2 = merged.split() # Back to two MultiSims with 3 runs each (or use inds or chunks to split another way)
```

## Copies

Both `ss.Sim` and `ss.MultiSim` objects let you control whether or not the objects passed into them are copied. By default, sims _do_ copy inputs and multisims _don't_. Let's look at a few examples.

Sims copy inputs by default because it's common to want to reuse a module between sims, which wouldn't be allowed if it wasn't copied (since it's modified in place during run). For example:

```{python}
sis = ss.SIS(beta=0.1)

s1 = ss.Sim(label='Low contacts', n_agents=2000, diseases=sis, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=5))
s2 = ss.Sim(label='High contacts', n_agents=2000, diseases=sis, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10))
ss.parallel(s1, s2).plot()
```

But this can be confusing, because it means the `sis` in the simulation is a different object than the `sis` you created. If you want to keep it the same, set `copy_inputs=False`, for example, to use it directly afterwards:

```{python}
sir = ss.SIR(beta=0.035)
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases=sir, networks='random', copy_inputs=False)
sim.run()
sir.plot() # This wouldn't work without copy_inputs=False
```

Conversely, `ss.MultiSim()` by default does _not_ copy the input sims, so they are modified in place:

```{python}
s1 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks='random')
s2 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sir', networks='random')
ss.parallel(s1, s2, verbose=0)

s1.plot() # This also works, because it was run in place
```

If you want to copy the sims before run, then set `inplace=False`:

```{python}
s1 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sis', networks='random')
s2 = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sir', networks='random')
ss.parallel(s1, s2, verbose=0, inplace=False)

s1.run().plot() # This now works, because the sim was *not* run in place
```

## Reducing memory use

When you run many simulations and keep them all in memory (or save them to disk), the biggest contributor to the size of each `Sim` is usually the `People` object and the per-agent state arrays. Once a run has finished, you typically only need the results, not the full population. Calling `sim.shrink()` removes these memory-intensive attributes in place, keeping the results intact:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
import sciris as sc

# Run a reasonably large sim
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=5000, diseases='sis', networks='random', verbose=0).run()

# Compare the size before and after shrinking
before = len(sc.dumpstr(sim))
sim.shrink()
after = len(sc.dumpstr(sim))
print(f'Size before shrinking: {before/1e6:.2f} MB')
print(f'Size after shrinking:  {after/1e6:.2f} MB')

# Results are still available
sim.plot('sis')
```

:::{.callout-tip}
It's good practice to call `sim.shrink()` (or `msim.shrink()` for a `MultiSim`) before storing or saving sims you've finished running, especially when running hundreds or thousands of them. This keeps memory use down and makes saved files smaller and faster to load. `ss.MultiSim` and `ss.parallel()` already shrink each sim by default, so you only need to do this for sims you run and store yourself.
:::

If you later need the full sim (for example, to continue running it), don't shrink it — or save it with `sim.save('mysim.sim', shrink=False)` to keep everything.

## Advanced workflows

A common pattern for more complex workflows is to write `make_sim()`. The example below, based on an STIsim application, shows how complex a `make_sim()` function can get (this is, after all, where most of the science happens!):

```py
def make_sim(seed=1, n_agents=None, start=1990, stop=2030, debug=False, add_stis=True, scenario='treat'):

    total_pop = {1970: 5.203e6, 1980: 7.05e6, 1985: 8.691e6, 1990: 9980999, 2000: 11.83e6}[start]
    if n_agents is None: n_agents = [int(10e3), int(5e2)][debug]
    dt = [ss.months(1), ss.years(1)][debug]

    # Demographic modules
    fertility_data = pd.read_csv(f'data/asfr.csv')
    pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(dt='month', fertility_rate=fertility_data)
    death_data = pd.read_csv(f'data/deaths.csv')
    death = ss.Deaths(death_rate=death_data, rate_units=1)

    # People and networks
    ppl = ss.People(n_agents, age_data=pd.read_csv(f'data/age_dist_{start}.csv', index_col='age')['value'])
    sexual = sti.FastStructuredSexual(
        prop_f0=0.79,
        prop_m0=0.83,
        f1_conc=0.16,
        m1_conc=0.11,
        p_pair_form=0.58,
        condom_data=pd.read_csv(f'data/condom_use.csv'),
    )
    maternal = ss.PrenatalNet(dt='month')

    # Diseases
    hiv = make_hiv()
    diseases = [hiv]
    if add_stis:
        ng, ct, tv, bv = make_stis()
        stis = [ng, ct, tv, bv]
        diseases += stis  # Add the STIs to the list of diseases

    # Interventions and analyzers
    intvs = make_hiv_intvs()
    if add_stis:
        intvs += make_testing(ng, ct, tv, bv, scenario=scenario, poc=poc, stop=stop)
        connectors = [sti.hiv_ng(hiv, ng), sti.hiv_ct(hiv, ct), sti.hiv_tv(hiv, tv)]
    else:
        connectors = []

    if analyzers is None:
        analyzers = [sti.sw_stats(diseases=['ng', 'ct', 'tv']), ts()]

    # Actually create the sim
    sim = ss.Sim(
        dt=dt,
        rand_seed=seed,
        total_pop=total_pop,
        start=str(start), # The year as a date string
        stop=str(stop),
        people=ppl,
        diseases=diseases,
        networks=[sexual, maternal],
        demographics=[pregnancy, death],
        interventions=intvs,
        analyzers=analyzers,
        connectors=connectors,
    )

    # Store scenario
    sim.scenario = scenario
    return sim
```

If your `make_sim()` function is computationally expensive, you can parallelize it using `sc.parallelize()`, e.g.

```py
# Make the arguments
iterkwargs = []
for seed in range(100):
    for n_agents in [1e3, 2e3, 5e3, 10e3]:
        iterkwargs.append(dict(seed=seed, n_agents=n_agents))

# Make the sims
sims = sc.parallelize(make_sim, iterkwargs=iterkwargs)
```
